speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. I see you are a pediatric patient presenting with a limp and localized pain, but no fever or acute distress. To begin our evaluation, can you tell me exactly where on your body the pain is located?

speaker: Patient
text: 7-year-old male. Mother has noticed a change in the child’s play patterns, specifically favoring his left leg while walking or running. The child complains of pain in his left knee, but denies any recent trauma or injury. He has no fever or other systemic symptoms. Nutrition and developmental milestones are appropriate for age.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for that detail. Since he is a 7-year-old boy with left knee pain and a limp but no trauma or fever, could you tell me if the pain actually feels like it's in the knee, or does he point to his hip or thigh when asked?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Pain localized to the left knee. I also have Limping favoring left leg, No fever, No systemic symptoms.

speaker: Doctor
text: That is helpful; however, in children, knee pain is often referred from the hip. Since the pain is localized to the left knee, I need to check for joint effusion and range of motion. Please have him lie down and let me examine his left knee and hip. REQUEST TEST: Physical_Exam_Legs_Hip

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Vital Signs: Temperature 36.8°C (98.2°F), Blood Pressure 100/65 mmHg, Heart Rate 82 bpm, Respiratory Rate 18 breaths/min. Musculoskeletal Examination: Inspection shows no visible deformity, swelling, or bruising of the knee or hip. Palpation reveals tenderness on the left hip, not the knee. Range of Motion is full in the knee; pain is elicited with passive motion of the hip. Special tests (anterior drawer and McMurray's) are negative, suggesting no knee joint instability or meniscal tear. Imaging (X-ray Left Hip) shows flattening and fragmentation of the left femoral head consistent with Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Legg-Calvé-Perthes Disease. The X-ray findings of femoral head fragmentation and flattening, combined with hip tenderness and referred knee pain in a 7-year-old boy, confirm this diagnosis. No further testing is required.
